We start by noting the key features of the presentation: an 8‐year‐old boy with a 3‐day history of fever, significant pain, and a rash on the trunk that includes several fragile bullous lesions. Many of these bullae have already eroded, leaving underlying erythematous lesions that have an annular (“target-like”) appearance. His general appearance (febrile, shaking, and evidently very sick) raises concern for a severe systemic process rather than a benign or localized skin infection.

Let’s briefly review the options:

• Bullous impetigo is a very common superficial bacterial infection in children caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Although it can present with fluid-filled bullae that are fragile, it usually is a relatively localized infection without significant systemic symptoms (like the marked fever and systemic illness seen in this patient).

• Autoimmune bullous dermatoses (such as pemphigus or pemphigoid) are rare in young children and tend to be chronic; they are usually not associated with an acute febrile, painful, rapidly evolving rash.

• Bullous erythema multiforme can occur in children (often triggered by infections such as herpes or Mycoplasma pneumoniae) and may present with target-like lesions. However, while erythema multiforme is typically limited to the extremities (hand–foot–face), in severe cases (erythema multiforme major) it involves mucosal surfaces and may look similar to SJS. Importantly, classic bullous impetigo and bullous erythema multiforme have a more limited regional distribution and do not usually present with such an acute systemic illness.

• Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a severe, acute mucocutaneous reaction (most commonly triggered by a medication or an infection) that often begins with fever and malaise, followed by the development of tender, bullous lesions that may rupture and leave behind raw, erythematous “target” or annular lesions. It almost always involves mucosal surfaces (such as the eyes, mouth, and genitals), and its systemic severity (fever, pain, and shaking chills) matches the presentation here—even though the mucosal involvement wasn’t explicitly noted in this brief exam, it may not have been obvious or the primary focus during the initial assessment.

Given the systemic symptoms (high fever and shaking), the rapid evolution (3‐day history), the fragile nature of the bullae, and the description of annular (target-like) lesions following blister erosion, the findings are most consistent with Stevens–Johnson syndrome.

Therefore, the final answer is: 

  \boxed{D}

We start by noting the key features in the case: a 52‐year‐old with a several‐year history of localized, very pruritic, hyperpigmented papules on both shins that “coalesce” to form thin, rippled plaques. There is no accompanying systemic disease, no medications, and no other skin problems.

Let’s look at the choices one‐by‐one:

• Hypertrophic lichen planus is classically described as flat, polygonal, violaceous papules (often with Wickham’s striae) and typically affects the wrists, shins, ankles, and genitals. It usually has a violaceous color rather than the hyperpigmented (brownish) lesions seen here, and the histopathology (with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and Civatte bodies) would not match this presentation.

• Pretibial myxedema almost always is seen in association with thyroidautoimmune disease (especially Graves’ disease) and appears as a thickened, edematous (peau d’orange–like) induration on the anterior shins. It is usually not very pruritic and lacks the papular rippled pattern described.

• Prurigo nodularis is characterized by nodular lesions (often 1–2 cm in diameter) arising in response to chronic itch; these nodules tend to be firm, hyperkeratotic (with a central keratin plug), and may exude chronic excoriation. While they can be extremely pruritic, their description as “thin, rippled plaques” that are hyperpigmented does not match the typical nodular appearance.

• Lichen amyloidosis (a localized form of cutaneous amyloidosis) typically presents as small, pruritic, hyperpigmented papules that often occur on extensor surfaces such as the shins. Over time these papules can coalesce and appear as thin, rippled plaques with underlying changes (e.g. slight hyperkeratosis). It is a chronic condition that can mimic a form of lichen simplex chronicus but is distinguished by the deposition of amyloid in the papillary dermis. Importantly, its history and distribution match exactly the features presented here.

Because the clinical picture (chronic pruritus of 3 years’ duration on the shins with hyperpigmented, rippled plaques and no systemic involvement) fits best with a chronic pruritic, localized dermatosis of the type seen in cutaneous amyloidosis, the best answer is:

\boxed{A}

We start by noting the “triple‐hit” of classic findings in zinc‐deficiency: painful, sharply demarcated eczematous lesions around the orifices (perioral/perianal) and on the hands/feet; failure to thrive with diarrhea; and progressive alopecia plus nail changes (nail dystrophy, paronychia). These features are characteristic of zinc deficiency. Importantly, the infant was doing well on breast milk – which is very bioavailable in zinc – until 2 months ago when he was switched to formula. (In premature infants the higher zinc requirements may not be met by some formulas.) 

This case does not look like “typical” atopic dermatitis (which involves flexural skin but usually responds to steroids), nor is it a mild “AE‐like” eruption that “mimics” AE without being due to zinc deficiency. Rather, his newly‐developed rash plus these systemic symptoms in the setting of “weaning” (i.e. switching from breast milk to less–bioavailable formula) makes an acquired zinc‐deficient state likely. When an otherwise normal infant develops a “Z‐deficit” (with the classic clinical triad of diarrhea, periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, nail changes, etc.) the term used is “acrodermatitis enteropathica‐like eruption” (AELE).

Thus, the most likely diagnosis is not genetic (inherited) acrodermatitis enteropathica (which would have presented when zinc demand first rose in breast–fed infants) but rather an acquired AELE (zinc deficiency induced by the feeding change).

So the final answer is: 

  \boxed{B}

• Location: It is on the front of the left knee and is completely subcutaneous with no overlying skin changes.

• Size: The mass is 8 cm in diameter, which is large but not unheard of for a benign growth.

Now let’s briefly consider each option:

A. Lipoma  
A lipoma is a common, benign tumor of the fat cells that usually appears as a soft, movable, subcutaneous mass. Large or “giant” lipomas can reach 8 cm in diameter and sometimes can be firmer than usual, but they are still classically present as a solitary mass without overlying skin changes—and they tend not to be very painful unless they press on a nerve. This fits the patient's history and physical exam.

B. Ganglion Cyst  
Ganglion cysts are fluid-filled cystic masses that attach to a tendon or joint capsule. They are typically soft (cystic), compressible, and sometimes even transilluminable. Although they can occur near the knee, they are usually not as firm as described, and a large 8 cm ganglion would be uncommon in presentation.

C. Synovial Cyst  
Synovial (or Baker’s) cysts are fluid-filled cysts that arise from the joint capsule (commonly behind the knee) and tend to be more cystic than solid. They are also not usually found on the front of the knee and rarely present as a firm subcutaneous mass.

D. Pigmented Villonodular Synovitis (PVNS)  
PVNS is a synovial disorder that occurs in and around a joint, sometimes causing joint pain, effusion, and limited motion. Although it can present as a slowly enlarging mass, it typically has an intra-articular component and might show brownish discoloration due to hemosiderin deposition. The location (completely subcutaneous on the front of the knee) and the simple, non-inflammatory presentation favor a mass that is not intra-articular in origin.

Because lipomas are the most common benign soft-tissue tumors and can present as a firm (sometimes even tender) isolated subcutaneous mass on the knee without the fluid nature or joint involvement seen with cysts or PVNS, the most likely diagnosis is:

  \boxed{A}

These findings point to a nutritional deficiency rather than a simple inflammatory or infectious process.

• Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease) presents with more generalized symptoms and distinct histological findings.
• Jacquet's dermatitis is not a well-defined term in this clinical context.

Thus, the constellation of a persistent diaper rash with peri-oral and tongue changes, unresponsive to standard treatment, and the nutritional history strongly supports a diagnosis of Acrodermatitis enteropathica.

Thus, putting all these pieces together, the most likely diagnosis for this patient is tuberous sclerosis complex.
